title: Lab Instrument Integration: How to Compare Informatics Options
summary: Compare API, file and integration-layer options for laboratory instrument integration. Plan sample mapping, error handling, evidence and ownership.
body_markdown:
The right laboratory instrument integration is the one that moves the required data, preserves its meaning, and handles failures predictably. An API is not always available. A file transfer is not always insufficient. The choice depends on the instrument software, supported interfaces, scientific context and destination workflow.


Before comparing platforms, define the complete journey: source output → sample and method context → transformation → checks → review → accepted result. Moving a file is only one step. A successful connection also explains what the data belongs to and whether it is ready to use.


## Compare integration patterns, not just connector counts


The following matrix is a design aid for laboratory instrument integration. Confirm every option against the installed software version and vendor-supported interfaces.


PatternUseful whenMain tradeoffTest before acceptanceSupported API or web serviceStructured records and permitted operations are availableVersion, permission and rate constraintsReads and writes obey business rulesControlled file ingestionThe instrument exports agreed filesExport timing and format changesPartial, repeated and revised filesVendor-supported database accessApproved views expose needed informationSchema and upgrade dependenceAccess scope and change compatibilityIntegration or orchestration layerMany systems share recurring flowsAdds an operating componentMonitoring, recovery and ownershipManual controlled handoffNo supported automated path is feasible yetContinued human effortTraceability and reconciliation


Direct database writes should not be the default shortcut. Require vendor approval and evidence that the route preserves the relevant application behavior. A successful SQL statement does not prove that required workflow rules ran.


A[scientific integration layer (GLUE)](https://www.scispot.com/glue) can be one pattern to evaluate when several sources share recurring flows.\[2\] A related discussion of[build versus buy in a hybrid model](https://www.scispot.com/blog/choosing-the-right-path-for-laboratory-instrument-integration-a-hybrid-model) may help frame that choice. It does not replace a test of your actual interface.


## Inspect the real source before designing the connection


Collect representative files, not only a polished example. Include failed runs, missing values, amended results, different methods and output from more than one device where relevant. Record software versions and export settings.


Decide what must travel with each result: sample identifier, run identifier, instrument identity, method and version, acquisition time, units, processing version, and quality status. Not every field comes from the instrument. Some context may need to be joined from the LIMS, ELN or an approved run manifest.


Document which fields are authoritative. A filename might help locate data, but it should not silently override a controlled sample identifier. When sources disagree, route the conflict rather than making an invisible guess.


## Separate raw capture from accepted results


Design distinct states for received, parsed, matched, checked, reviewed and published data. This prevents “file received” from being mistaken for “result approved.”


Retain the source and record the mapping or calculation version used to create a downstream value. If a reviewer asks why a concentration changed, the workflow should show whether the input, calculation, unit conversion or approval state changed.


For drug CGMP workflows, 21 CFR 211.194 addresses laboratory records and the data supporting testing.\[1\] Translate the applicable record obligations into the specific flow with Quality; do not assume a connector’s presence resolves them. Product capabilities for[instrument data automation](https://www.scispot.com/instrument-data-automation) are useful only when they support that record design.


## Design failure handling as part of the product


A practical acceptance set should include a file arriving twice, a transfer interrupted midway, an unknown sample, an unexpected unit, an unavailable destination, and an amended result arriving after approval.


For each case, specify the outcome. Duplicate delivery might be recognized using a stable event or source identifier. Incomplete input might stay quarantined. A failed write might retry with a limit and then alert an owner. An amendment might create a controlled new version rather than overwrite the accepted record.


Use reconciliation to compare expected and received records. An interface that reports no errors may still have missed an entire delivery. Monitoring should answer both “Did anything fail?” and “Did everything expected arrive?”


## Illustrative example: chromatography results into a LIMS


A laboratory creates sample requests in a LIMS. A chromatography data system holds run data and processed results. Analysts currently export results and enter values manually.


The proposed instrument to LIMS integration reads approved request context, associates each exported result with a sample and run, checks required fields, and routes exceptions to a reviewer. It writes permitted result fields through the destination’s supported mechanism. Raw and processed records remain traceable. Worklist creation is a separate requirement, not an automatic consequence of result import. A related[instrument file to final report](https://www.scispot.com/blog/instrument-file-to-final-report) pattern can inform the test cases.


Measure unmatched records, repeated submissions, time from approved source result to LIMS availability, and recovery time after a failed transfer. This is an illustrative architecture, not a claim of a prebuilt connector or a delivered customer result.


## Decide who will own the connection after activation


An instrument software update can change an export. A destination field can become mandatory. A new assay can introduce units the mapping did not anticipate. Treat these as change scenarios to plan for, not reasons to promise a maintenance-free integration.


The operating agreement should identify the owner of the source, destination and connection. Define alert routing, the supported operating window, access reviews, mapping changes, regression tests and recovery procedures. Distinguish response time from resolution time.


Before buying a new integration layer, ask whether existing infrastructure can operate the flow safely. Before choosing internal build, account for testing, monitoring, documentation and maintenance—not only the first parser.


## How Scispot can help connect the full workflow


Scispot’s role in laboratory instrument integration is to connect the data with the sample, method, checks and next approved action, often through a[lab operating layer](https://www.scispot.com/labos) . The lab can retain systems that already work.


[GLUE](https://www.scispot.com/glue) describes supported source intake, transformations and connected scientific data flows.\[2\] Those capabilities can support a scoped instrument-to-result workstream after the exact instrument software, available interface, permissions and acceptance criteria have been confirmed. Related[laboratory systems integration services](https://www.scispot.com/scientific-informatics-services) can be discussed once that first connection is defined.


For platforms such as LabVantage, the vendor documents web-service integration options. That establishes a possible integration route, not universal access to every installed function.\[3\]


[Book a Free Consultation](https://www.scispot.com/demo-request) . Bring representative files and a clear destination outcome.


## Key takeaway


Choose a laboratory instrument integration approach that preserves context and fails visibly. The goal is a trusted result in the right workflow, not simply a moving file.
